cited_evidence.text: Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

decision.trend: Research has been focused on designing high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with improved ductility, strength, and resistance to radiation damage. Various processing techniques such as arc melting, selective laser melting, and laser powder bed fusion have been employed to produce HEAs with unique microstructures and properties. The addition of alloying elements and the control of processing parameters have been shown to enhance the ductility and strength of HEAs. Furthermore, the use of high-pressure and high-temperature treatment has been explored to overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in eutectic high entropy alloys.
decision.unsolved: Despite the progress made, there is still a need to understand the underlying mechanisms that control the ductility and strength of HEAs, particularly in relation to their microstructure and chemical composition. Additionally, the development of HEAs with improved radiation resistance and thermal stability remains a challenge.
decision.why: The next step would be to design a controlled variable experiment to investigate the effect of processing parameters, such as laser power, scanning speed, and layer thickness, on the microstructure and properties of HEAs. This would help to establish a clear understanding of the relationships between processing, microstructure, and properties, and ultimately lead to the development of HEAs with optimized ductility, strength, and radiation resistance.
